headline: Cost-of-Living Pressure and Arms Bill Dispute Dominate New Zealand Parliament
summary: The House heard sharp challenges over the cost of living for Pasifika families, rising benefit numbers and child hardship, while ministers defended the Government’s economic and welfare record. MPs also advanced the Arms Bill through committee with amendments, amid debate over the new firearms regulator, and questioned the Government on climate targets, road spending and the handling of a company briefing document.

topicSummaries.topic: Pasifika Cost-of-Living Pressures Put to Government
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: Rising grocery and household energy costs affect families’ ability to meet everyday expenses, particularly when they have little financial room for unexpected bills.
topicSummaries.content: Labour deputy leader Carmel Sepuloni challenged the Government’s promise to help Pacific communities navigate the cost of living, citing increases over two years of 26 percent for milk, 32 percent for potatoes, 28 percent for mince, 67 percent for white bread and 26 percent for household energy. She also referred to survey figures showing many Pasifika people could not cover an unexpected $500 bill and had taken on debt. Responding on behalf of the Minister for Pacific Peoples, Tama Potaka acknowledged significant challenges but pointed to employment gains, higher school attendance and Whānau Ora support, and said the Government was focused on strengthening the economy.

keyExchanges.speaker: Hon Carmel Sepuloni (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: Has the Government kept its promise to help Pacific communities actually navigate the cost of living when milk prices are up 26 percent, potatoes are up 32 percent, mince is up 28 percent, and white bread is up 67 percent in the last two years?

keyExchanges.speaker: Hon Tama Potaka (National)
keyExchanges.quote: There are a number of challenges that Pasifika and many other whānau across Aotearoa New Zealand are facing, and that’s why we are so geared to ensure that we fix the economy in a manner that endures.

topicSummaries.topic: Jobseeker Target and Child Hardship Draw Labour and Green Criticism
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: Employment and child poverty figures speak directly to household security and whether families can afford basic needs.
topicSummaries.content: Social Development and Employment Minister Louise Upston reaffirmed a target to reduce the number of people receiving jobseeker support by 50,000 by 2030, saying improved economic conditions and employment programmes would help. Labour’s Willow-Jean Prime challenged her with figures showing jobseeker numbers had risen since the Government took office and questioned whether ministry forecasts put the target out of reach. Green MP Kahurangi Carter highlighted that many children experiencing material hardship belong to working families and cited a rise in hardship; Upston emphasised employment as a route out of poverty and pointed to more than $90 million in Budget 2026 funding to help sole parents into work.

keyExchanges.speaker: Hon Willow-Jean Prime (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: Do the Ministry of Social Development’s own forecasts show she will miss her target by 60,000 people by 2030?

keyExchanges.speaker: Hon Louise Upston (National)
keyExchanges.quote: I’m really focused on our target to reduce the number of people on the jobseeker benefit, and, as I say, this Government is absolutely focused on growing the economy so there are a growing number of jobs available—Budget 2026, 220,000 new jobs—so I’m confident that we will continue to make progress on our jobseeker target.

keyExchanges.speaker: Kahurangi Carter (Green)
keyExchanges.quote: How does she reconcile that out of the nearly 170,000 children living in material hardship in New Zealand, half of them belong to working families?

keyExchanges.speaker: Hon Louise Upston (National)
keyExchanges.quote: What we do know is that we want to have a growing economy so more New Zealanders are in work with higher wages. That is absolutely how we pull people out of poverty.

topicSummaries.topic: Arms Bill Advances After Committee Approves Government Amendments
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The bill would change firearms licensing, offences and administration, affecting licence holders, firearms businesses and the agencies responsible for public safety.
topicSummaries.content: The committee of the whole House approved the Arms Bill’s Parts 3 to 8 and schedules, including government amendments, and reported the bill back to the House; it is set down for a third reading next sitting day. Associate Justice Minister Nicole McKee said amendments included revised penalties, provisions covering restricted ammunition and the establishment of a firearms regulator separate from Police for administrative functions, with Police retaining enforcement responsibilities. Opposition amendments seeking greater Police involvement in regulator appointments and other changes were rejected. MPs also debated safeguards, information-sharing, officers’ identification and the bill’s commencement dates; most provisions are due to take effect on 23 September 2026, with some later changes dependent on IT development.

keyExchanges.speaker: Vanushi Walters (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: I would suggest, on the basis of the Minister’s explanation, that that absolutely makes sense.

keyExchanges.speaker: Hon Nicole McKee (ACT)
keyExchanges.quote: I reject all of the member Ginny Andersen’s proposed amendments. As I had earlier mentioned, 90 percent of submitters who submitted on this particular proposal are in favour of the separation of New Zealand Police from the firearms administrator or regulator, and every single one of those proposals that the member’s put forward means that there would be no separation, and that is not the intent of this particular part.

keyExchanges.speaker: Dr Lawrence Xu-Nan (Green)
keyExchanges.quote: However, we have seen those kind of genuine improvements that have been made through this process.

keyExchanges.speaker: Hon Nicole McKee (ACT)
keyExchanges.quote: The commencement date of 23 September 2026 is doable. Both organisations, New Zealand Police and the Firearm Safety Authority, have been working towards that date.

topicSummaries.topic: Climate Targets Challenged as Green Urgent Debate Is Declined
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The Government’s emissions plans shape energy and transport policy and the pace of action on climate change.
topicSummaries.content: Green MP Francisco Hernandez cited the Climate Change Commission’s assessment that several indicators had worsened and that the second emissions reduction plan was at significant risk. Climate Change Minister Simon Watts said Government projections showed New Zealand on track to meet its first two emissions budgets and net zero by 2050, pointing to renewable energy projects and lower gross emissions in 2024. He said the Government would formally respond to the commission’s report in October. The Speaker declined Hernandez’s request for an urgent debate, ruling that the report did not meet the procedural test for a recent matter requiring immediate attention.

keyExchanges.speaker: Francisco Hernandez (Green)
keyExchanges.quote: Why does he remain confident that the Government remains on track when the Climate Change Commission’s report has found that the second emissions reduction plan is at “significant risk” due to actions like the proposed liquefied natural gas terminal, cancellation of the clean car discounts, and scrapping pricing for biogenic methane emissions?

keyExchanges.speaker: Hon Simon Watts (National)
keyExchanges.quote: Well, the Government will formally respond to the Climate Change Commission’s report in October, but in the interim, I can be very clear to that member is that this is a Government that is focused on delivery and that the fast-track process and the amount of new renewable generation projects is a fundamental shift in the landscape in this country that will power our economy and also ensure that we deliver clean energy, which achieves both outcomes of economic growth and emissions reduction.

topicSummaries.topic: $323.8M Spent on Road Pre-Implementation Work, Minister Says
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The scale and timing of transport spending affect taxpayers and motorists, while construction delays can leave promised regional projects uncertain.
topicSummaries.content: Transport Minister Chris Bishop told the House that $323.8 million had been spent by 30 April on pre-implementation work for roads of national significance not yet in procurement or construction. He clarified that $90 million of the $675 million approved in October 2025 had been spent on six named projects, and apologised for an error in an earlier written answer. Labour’s Tangi Utikere questioned spending on projects without guaranteed construction dates and raised motorists’ costs. Bishop said the projects had not been cancelled, defended planning and consent work as necessary to build a pipeline, and said construction timelines for some projects remained unfinalised.

keyExchanges.speaker: Tangi Utikere (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: Does he stand by his view that the hundreds of millions spent planning roads with no construction date is “not a waste”, but “an investment in the future”, particularly given the RONS projects in phases 2 and 3 have, effectively, been cancelled by his Government?

keyExchanges.speaker: Hon Chris Bishop (National)
keyExchanges.quote: Firstly, to start with the last assertion, they have not been cancelled—they are Government priorities—and, secondly, they are not a waste.

keyExchanges.speaker: Tangi Utikere (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: Why should motorists, who are already paying $50 more in registration fees and facing petrol tax hikes, believe that any of that money will buy them anything other than more consultancy reports, like the $323.8 million he has already spent?

keyExchanges.speaker: Hon Chris Bishop (National)
keyExchanges.quote: The reality is: we try and put the best use of fuel tax revenue to its highest-value use, and that is what we’ll continue to do.

topicSummaries.topic: Minister Cites 25-Year Low in Annual Rent Increases
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: Rent trends affect the budgets of tenants, students and families, while housing affordability influences the ability to find and keep a home.
topicSummaries.content: Housing Minister Chris Bishop cited Stats NZ figures showing annual rent increases of 0.5 percent in the year to June, which he described as the lowest rate in 25 years. He also said new-tenancy rents had remained flat since November 2023 and reported that first-home buyers accounted for a record share of purchases in the June quarter. Bishop attributed improved affordability indicators to making it easier to build and increasing the supply of developable land. These figures and assessments were presented by the minister in response to questions from a National MP.

topicSummaries.topic: Labour Questions Learning First’s Role in Curriculum Rewrite
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: Curriculum design affects what students are taught and how much influence overseas contractors have in shaping New Zealand’s education system.
topicSummaries.content: Labour’s Ginny Andersen questioned Education Minister Erica Stanford about the Australian company Learning First’s involvement in the curriculum rewrite, citing ministry communications that she said referred to input across learning areas and review of curriculum content. Stanford maintained that the company was contracted to advise on benchmarking, quality assurance and knowledge-rich curriculum frameworks, while hundreds of New Zealanders wrote the curriculum and drafts were consulted on. Stanford said the difference was between influencing the work and writing it, and that final curriculum areas would be released after feedback was considered.

keyExchanges.speaker: Hon Ginny Andersen (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: Why, then, did the Ministry report to the Minister in July 2025 that Learning First was involved to a point where they were reviewing the curriculum content and, in fact, advising the Ministry of Education not to consult with our education sector on the draft curriculum because it would be “disruptive”?

keyExchanges.speaker: Hon Erica Stanford (National)
keyExchanges.quote: I haven’t seen that, but what I know is that the company was contracted, as I’ve already said, to do those things, and part of that work was the parameters of a knowledge-rich curriculum, understanding what a knowledge-rich curriculum is, which is what the Ministry of Education needed advice with across multiple areas of the curriculum.

keyExchanges.speaker: Hon Ginny Andersen (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: How can she continue to hold her head up and state that Learning First did not write the school curriculum when reports signed out by her show they directly influenced it?

keyExchanges.speaker: Hon Erica Stanford (National)
keyExchanges.quote: Well, I think the answer to that question is clear in the member’s question: there’s a difference between writing and influence.

topicSummaries.topic: Questions Raised Over Hand-Delivered Z Energy Briefing
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: Public confidence in government decision-making depends on clear processes for handling lobbying material and access to official information.
topicSummaries.content: Labour’s Camilla Belich questioned the Government about media reports that a Z Energy briefing note preceding the Climate Change Response (Tort Liability) Amendment Bill was hand-delivered after a request from the Prime Minister’s office. Acting for the Justice Minister, James Meager said he was aware of reports but would not give an opinion on another office’s actions or assess whether the circumstances complied with the Official Information Act. He said such matters could be considered by the Ombudsman. The Speaker rejected Labour’s point of order that the minister was required to provide a view.

keyExchanges.speaker: Camilla Belich (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: Does he accept that a Minister’s office asking for a lobbying document to be delivered by hand could circumvent the Official Information Act, for which he has responsibility as Minister of Justice?

keyExchanges.speaker: Hon James Meager (National), on behalf of the Minister of Justice
keyExchanges.quote: My understanding is that while the Ministry of Justice is responsible for the administration of the Act, in terms of individual actions under that Act, that is for, I think, the Ombudsman to inquire into and not the Minister of Justice.

conclusion: The Arms Bill advanced with the Government’s amendments intact, while disputes over household costs, welfare outcomes, climate policy and government accountability remained unresolved.
